title: Kickoff notes — Dedicated throughput SLO + tier definitions
content:
Meeting: Dedicated throughput SLO + tier definitions — kickoff
Date/time: 2025-01-14 10:00–11:00 PT
Location: Zoom
Notes owner: Lauren Bishop

Why we’re here (Lauren)
- Dedicated customers keep asking for “guaranteed throughput,” but we’re currently inconsistent across:
  - Sales proposals / order forms (“you’ll get X tokens/sec”) vs.
  - Runtime behavior under load (batching/backpressure) vs.
  - SRE’s ability to alert + attribute cause (customer traffic vs platform vs supply).
- This project aims to define:
  1) what “throughput” means + how we measure it,
  2) tier definitions with enforceable policies,
  3) mapping to hardware shapes + regional availability,
  4) the reporting surface and escalation path,
  5) contract/SLA language and remedies.

Attendees / stakeholders
- Product: Lauren Bishop (DRI), Evelyn Hart (exec sponsor), Talia Benson (PgM support)
- Runtime: Sofia Ivanova (scheduling), Noah Patel (arch), Omar El-Sayed (throughput owner)
- Infra/Fleet: Irene Choi (sponsor), Vanessa Ortiz (capacity lead)
- SRE/SLO governance: Rafael Mendes (lead), Aisha Bello (alerting/error budgets)
- GTM: Jordan Blake (GTM sponsor)
- CS: Jasmine Liu (CS sponsor)
- Legal: Michael Grant (Legal sponsor), Sofia Mendes (commercial counsel)

High-level outcomes we want by end of project (group)
- One sentence definition of throughput for Dedicated + published measurement standard reference.
- Tier matrix (Standard / Performance / Premium) with:
  - objective (sustained throughput),
  - measurement window,
  - exclusions,
  - burst semantics (what’s allowed; what happens when exceeded),
  - operational policies (admission control, overload mode).
- Shape catalog mapping per tier + explicit region availability constraints.
- Dashboards + a customer-visible export (or at minimum, a customer report) so “did we meet it?” isn’t subjective.
- Exception process: when Sales asks for a one-off guarantee, what approvals/pricing uplift are required.

Customer problem recap (Jordan + Jasmine)
- The ask is not just “faster.” It’s predictability:
  - Customers want to size their application capacity + know what they’re paying for.
  - They want to avoid “it depends” answers when latency/throughput degrades.
- Common misalignment:
  - Customer assumes tokens/sec across any prompt mix; we know prefill dominates for long contexts.
  - Customer assumes they can burst 10x for free; we know that creates queueing and tail latency spikes.
- CS pain point: escalations get stuck in loop between Support → SRE → Runtime without an agreed SLO definition and a standard dashboard to point to.

Initial tier strawman (NOT final)
Working names: Standard / Performance / Premium

Dimension ideas
- Primary objective: sustained output token throughput (tokens/sec) under a defined workload profile.
- Secondary guardrails: tail latency bounds (not necessarily SLA’ed at first, but used to prevent “meet throughput by destroying latency”).
- Concurrency assumptions: must be explicitly stated per tier.
- Burst: bounded and governed (either token bucket / concurrency burst / short-duration sustained).

Strawman tier semantics (rough)
- Standard:
  - Conservative sustained throughput objective; minimal burst.
  - Goal: price-sensitive customers who just want “noisy neighbor” removed + baseline predictability.
  - Throttling behavior is expected before SLO breach (admission control kicks in).
- Performance:
  - Higher sustained objective; some burst allowance.
  - More aggressive autoscaling/burst capacity options (where fleet supply allows).
  - Better reporting/visibility.
- Premium:
  - Highest sustained objective + faster mitigation response.
  - Restricted shapes/regions (supply dependent).
  - Potentially stronger remedies / SLA commitments.

Notes from Infra (Irene, Vanessa)
- Shape availability is going to constrain tiers more than we’d like.
  - Premium can’t be “available everywhere.” We need published region constraints.
  - We should avoid promises that require last-minute reshuffling across customers.
- We should decide early:
  - MIG vs no-MIG policy for Dedicated tiers (default: no-MIG unless a specific tier uses it for binpacking).
  - Single-node vs multi-node requirements (NVLink/IB) and whether we even support multi-node in first tier set.

Notes from Runtime (Sofia, Noah, Omar)
- Throughput is sensitive to:
  - prompt/context distribution (prefill)
  - streaming vs non-streaming
  - decode length distribution
  - tool/function calling patterns (stop/start)
- We can measure tokens/sec, but we need to specify:
  - whether it is output-only tokens or total (input+output)
  - whether we report “effective tokens/sec” including time spent waiting/queued
- Guardrails:
  - Admission control is the enforcement mechanism; otherwise “guarantee” is not operational.
  - Overload mode: we need a clear definition of when to throttle, and what “expected throttling” looks like for customer-visible behavior.

SRE perspective (Rafael, Aisha)
- A measurable SLO needs:
  - an SLI definition that’s stable and not too gameable
  - a window (rolling 5m? 15m?) that matches customer expectations and alert practicality
  - explicit exclusions: scheduled maintenance, customer-induced errors, warmup, misconfiguration, etc.
- We need to decide:
  - Whether the “SLO miss” is when observed throughput < objective OR when we fail to provide the capacity due to platform issue.
  - How to classify an event when the system throttled correctly: likely “not an SLO breach,” but we need language + customer comms.

Open questions (capture for PRD/ADRs)
1) Primary metric choice
- Tokens/sec vs requests/sec
  - Tokens/sec matches cost + GPU utilization, but customers think in req/s sometimes.
  - Proposal: tokens/sec is primary; req/s can be derived/reporting-only.
- Output tokens/sec vs total tokens/sec
  - Output-only is closer to “what customer gets,” but input/prefill cost is real.
  - Consider: SLI = sustained output tokens/sec, with workload profile including input/output token distributions.

2) Measurement window + aggregation
- Rolling window options: 1m, 5m, 15m.
  - Short windows are noisy; long windows hide pain.
- Percentiles
  - Do we define objective at p50? p95? min?
  - Concern: “p95 throughput” is confusing; throughput is a rate over time.
  - Alternative: define as (tokens_out / wall_clock_time) over rolling window, then take pX over windows.

3) Workload assumptions
- We need a “standard workload profile” per tier and/or per model class:
  - context length buckets
  - output length distribution
  - concurrency pattern
  - streaming vs non-streaming
- Question: do tiers define a single workload profile, or do we define a baseline matrix by model family (e.g., 7B/13B/70B)?

4) Burst semantics
- What is “burst” exactly?
  - Short-term rate above sustained objective?
  - Concurrency above contracted baseline?
  - Temporary access to additional GPUs?
- How do we communicate burst to customers without implying unlimited capacity?
- How do we treat burst utilization in pricing (is it included, metered, or best-effort)?

5) Enforcement / overload behavior
- What happens when customer exceeds contracted throughput/concurrency?
  - 429/503 vs queueing vs increased latency.
  - For streaming, how does throttling manifest (slower token cadence vs delayed first token)?
- When do we “shed” vs “throttle”?
- How do we keep admission control from looking like “we failed the guarantee” when it’s actually protecting the SLO?

6) Remedies / SLA language
- If we miss the SLO due to Redwood fault, what’s the remedy?
  - Credit tied to duration and severity?
  - Cap on credits?
- Carve-outs:
  - customer misconfig, prompt spikes beyond contracted burst, upstream/downstream networking, scheduled maintenance, etc.

7) Console + reporting
- Minimum bar:
  - internal dashboard per deployment (throughput vs objective, throttling rate, queue depth)
  - a customer export/report (CSV/API) for the same SLI numbers
- Question: do we show real-time “currently meeting SLO” in console, or just historical compliance?

Initial decisions (tentative, subject to ADR)
- We should define throughput in tokens/sec, not req/s (req/s can be a derived/helpful metric).
- Admission control is part of the product promise; throttling under overload should be described as “expected behavior” when customers exceed tier assumptions.
- Tier availability must be region-bound; Premium likely limited at launch.

Milestones (proposal)
- Week 1–2: discovery + baseline
  - Gather top 5 customer workload patterns for Dedicated (Jordan/Jasmine to provide)
  - Run benchmarks on candidate shapes (Irene/Vanessa coordinate; Omar supports methodology)
  - Draft measurement standard (Aisha + Rafael with Omar)
- Week 2–4: spec + alignment
  - PRD v1 with tier matrix, exclusions, burst semantics (Lauren)
  - ADR for primary metric choice (Noah + Rafael)
  - ADR for tier semantics + burst policy (Lauren + Aisha + Sofia)
- Week 4–6: implementation planning
  - Instrumentation issues + labels (Logan to be pulled in; Sofia/Omar)
  - Dashboard panels and alerting policy (Sergio to be pulled in; Aisha)
- Week 6–8: launch readiness
  - Sales enablement cheat sheet + FAQ (Stephanie to be pulled in; Jordan + Lauren)
  - Contract language draft + review (Michael + Sofia Mendes)

Action items / owners
- Lauren: Draft PRD skeleton + list of open questions as a decision log (due 2025-01-17)
- Talia: Create shared tracker + schedule weekly working session (due 2025-01-16)
- Jordan: Provide 3–5 recent Dedicated deal examples where throughput was a key point (due 2025-01-20)
- Jasmine: Compile top support/CS themes re: throughput + examples of customer language (due 2025-01-20)
- Irene/Vanessa: Initial list of candidate shapes + region constraints for each (due 2025-01-21)
- Omar: Propose benchmark methodology for “tier baseline workload” (due 2025-01-21)
- Rafael/Aisha: Recommend SLO windowing + alerting approach (draft) (due 2025-01-23)
- Michael Grant + Sofia Mendes: Outline of SLA clause structure + key carve-outs to expect (due 2025-01-24)

Parking lot (items we didn’t get to)
- How to handle multi-model deployments (one Dedicated cluster serving multiple models) in measurement and tier eligibility.
- Whether we offer “model pinned” vs “compatible fallback model” within Dedicated tiers.
- How we handle planned maintenance windows for Dedicated (notification minimums + whether it counts against SLO).

Notes to self (Lauren)
- Keep this project anchored on enforceability: if we can’t measure and alert on it, we shouldn’t promise it.
- Make sure the tier definitions don’t accidentally encourage customers to optimize for tokens/sec at the expense of latency quality.
- Expect conflict between Sales wanting broad Premium availability and Fleet reality; get ahead with explicit region constraints.
